title: Four great vows
hook: beings are numberless, I vow to free them; delusions are endless, I vow to end them (as chanted in Zen)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother of the Buddhas: the perfection of wisdom, tended by the Buddhas the way grown children tend a mother who gave them the world. Your line: the mother of Buddhas. Whose good thing did you trace back? Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

The last bell of the evening sit rings in a Zen hall. Nobody stands up yet. Instead, the whole room starts to chant, together, in a low and even voice. The first line goes something like this: beings are numberless; I vow to free them. The second: delusions are endless; I vow to end them. Then two more lines, and the room goes quiet. Said slowly, it sounds calm. Heard closely, it sounds impossible. Numberless, and I vow. Endless, and I vow. Today: the four great vows.
screen: `THE LAST BELL.` → `THE ROOM CHANTS TOGETHER.` → `IMPOSSIBLE, AND VOWED.`

segments.voice: First, the four lines. English versions differ, and each community keeps its own, but the shape holds. Beings without number: I vow to free them. Delusions without end: I vow to end them. Gates of the teaching beyond measure: I vow to enter them. The Buddha's way, with nothing above it: I vow to become it. Four lines. Each one names something too large, and then makes a promise anyway. Second, why say something impossible. A vow you can finish is a task. A vow you can't finish is a direction. These aren't lines to tick off by Friday. They set the face of a life toward something, the way a compass points north without ever arriving there. The bodhisattva, earlier in this block, was one who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings. These four lines are that wish, said out loud, often, with other people. Third, why say it together, and again. In Zen and in other Mahayana communities, the vows are chanted at the end of a sit, at ceremonies, at the start of retreats. Said once, a vow is a decision. Said every evening, it becomes a habit of the heart, worn smooth like a stair. Fourth, where this week has been. It began with Samantabhadra and his great vows, then Maitreya, the one to come, then Ksitigarbha, who vows to help in the lowest places, then skillful means, the perfection of wisdom and its mother. Now the vows themselves, in four lines short enough to carry. Numberless, I vow. The first word admits the size of the job. The next two start it anyway.
screen: `FOUR LINES, ONE SHAPE.` · `A VOW YOU CAN'T FINISH IS A DIRECTION.` · `SAID TOGETHER, SAID AGAIN.` · `THIS WEEK, IN FOUR LINES.` · then, large: `NUMBERLESS, I VOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: the four vows, on four breaths. If you chant them, say them in the version your community uses, slowly, one line to a breath. If you don't, just let the shapes pass through. Breathe in, and on the out-breath: numberless. Next breath: endless. Next: beyond measure. Next: nothing above it. Then sit with whatever's left, the size of it, and the small steady breath that keeps going anyway. If your mind wanders, come back to the word numberless. The bell holds the time.
Four great vows. Beings, delusions, gates of the teaching, the Buddha's way: each too large, each vowed anyway. Chanted in Zen halls after the sit. Today's word.

Your line: numberless, I vow. Today, pick one thing too big to finish, and do one small piece of it anyway, without needing to see the end. Tomorrow, dedication. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

original.note: Sanskrit: a vow or resolve, the word for a bodhisattva's great vows.

trapdoor: what you thought: a vow is a promise you plan to keep and finish.
what it means: the four great vows name what can't be finished, beings without number, and vow anyway; they set a direction.
what a scholar hears: the four lines are the bodhisattva's wish in its shortest form, chanted in East Asian Mahayana, each community in its own wording.
